subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Japanese Tea Ceremony
description: A 60-second lesson on The Japanese Tea Ceremony.

hook.text: Sen no Rikyu perfected the Japanese tea ceremony in the 1580s. Every movement had meaning.

buildup.text: Guests crawl through a tiny door to enter the tea room—a gesture of humility, regardless of rank.

discovery.text: Rikyu's four principles: harmony, respect, purity, and tranquility. The tea is almost secondary.

twist.text: Rikyu was ordered to commit ritual suicide by the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi over a political dispute.

climax.text: His death made him a martyr. The tea ceremony he designed is still practiced unchanged 400+ years later.

punchline.text: The master died. His ceremony lives on, unchanged.

quiz.question: What are Rikyu's four principles of tea ceremony?

details.summary: The Japanese tea ceremony, chanoyu, is a ritualized preparation and serving of matcha rooted in Zen Buddhist principles. Developed by tea masters like Murata Juko and Sen no Rikyu in the 15th and 16th centuries, it emphasizes harmony, respect, purity, and tranquility. Every movement is intentional.
details.whyItMatters: The tea ceremony distills centuries of Japanese aesthetics and philosophy into a single ritual. It influenced architecture, ceramics, flower arrangement, and the global concept of mindfulness.
takeaways: Chanoyu is a Zen-influenced ritual of preparing matcha
Sen no Rikyu codified its principles in the 16th century
It embodies harmony, respect, purity, and tranquility

faq.question: How long does a full tea ceremony take?
faq.answer: A formal tea gathering, called chaji, lasts about four hours and includes a kaiseki meal, a break in the garden, thick tea served to the group, and thin tea served individually. A shorter version, chakai, lasts about an hour. Even the simplest version follows precise rituals.

faq.question: What are the four principles of the tea ceremony?
faq.answer: Wa means harmony between guests and nature. Kei is respect for all people and things. Sei is purity of heart and environment. Jaku is tranquility achieved through the practice of the other three. These principles guide every aspect of the ceremony from gesture to decor.
